doc.title: Ruth Brown interviewed by Michael Woods, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 4, 1995

title: Changing a lyric to turn a song into gospel
summary: Brown explains that swapping a word like 'love' for 'God' and slowing the tempo makes a song gospel, and recalls her mother's warning about hips and soul.

story.theme_name: Church, faith and religion in a musician's life
story.community_name: Church, faith and jazz: the sacred and the secular

blocks.x: That’s right. Oh, you play with God, will ya? And by the time she got through admonishing us, I said all that to say that there is this fine line and it had to do with the lyrics. Of course there’s a song that we do even now, “You’re the Best Thing That’s Ever Happened to Me.” In the church we say God is the best thing that’s ever happened to me. I did a song once called “I Can See Everybody’s Baby but I Can’t See Mine.” The Dixie Hummingbirds did it and it was called “I Can See Everybody’s Mother but I Don’t See Mine.” You see, it’s just about the lyrics. That’s all it is. And even now I can take any song and change one line, change one word, replace “love” or “darling” with “God.” Or “Our Father” and slow the tempo, lay it back, lay the tempo back, and it becomes Gospel spiritual.
You know there’s a, there’s a rendition of I think BeBe and CeCe [Winans] doing “Lord Lift Us Up Where We Belong” which was song a song from a movie.

That’s right. “Lord Lift Us Up Where We Belong,” and it makes sense, wouldn’t it? That was from “An Officer and a Gentleman” the song, it really was. Well as I said, it’s just the attitude that can change it. I mean like even coming up to sing Gospel and there’s a beat behind it. I made this statement that my mother used to say, “If it moves your hip and not your soul, be careful,” you know but you’ve really got to watch it nowadays, cause you’ll find without thinking you will move your hips to the music. I don’t think that God cares.
